new_statements.rule_in_words: As reported second-hand for Heine 1976: Nyang'i inherits Proto-Kuliak primary stress unchanged, and that primary stress was not tied to a fixed position (it 'could occur in any position'), i.e. its place is lexically given; a secondary stress falls on the second syllable of the word. This is a tertiary paraphrase of a comparative reconstruction, not a synchronic description of Nyang'i, and it could not be checked against Heine's text.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Second syllable of the word (Proto-Kuliak secondary stress 'remains there in Ik and Nyang'i'), per the same second-hand report.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Schrock 2014:100 adds that 'Tone data on Nyang'ía is not yet available', so it is unknown whether Nyang'i is tonal like Ik or stress-accent like So.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('of a word'); no information on citation forms vs phrases. The only modern description (Beer 2017) rests on one semi-speaker's contracted idiolect (Komol Isaach, Lobalangit, 2012-2014).
new_statements.identity_note: Nyang'i [nyan1313, nyp], Nyangea Mountains / Lobalangit, Karamoja, Uganda; Western Kuliak with Soo/Tepes. No dialect issue, but the sources describe different stages: Heine 1975/1976 worked with the last fluent speakers in the early 1970s, while Beer 2017 documents the contracted idiolect of a single semi-speaker (Komol Isaach, 2012-2014). Any stress statement from Beer 2017 would describe that idiolect.

new_statements.quote: p. 40-41: "I have not identified any two words in Nyang'i that differ in meaning solely on the basis of pitch. However, two factors suggest that pitch must be lexically specified for Nyang'i roots. First, the pitch features of a given root are not predictable on the basis of the phonological context [...]. Second, the pitch features of a given word-form are consistent across utterances [...]. Pitch is a feature that has an active role in the lexicon and grammar, but is never the sole means of contrast. Acoustic correlates of stress additional to pitch (i.e. duration and amplitude) do not correlate systematically with pitch (i.e. syllables with high pitch are not systematically longer or louder than syllables with low pitch), suggesting that the prosodic system is not more meaningfully described as a stress system than as a tone system." p. 20: "Pitch is not lexically or grammatically contrastive, but pitch features must be part of a speaker's lexical representation for each word, as they are unpredictable."

new_statements.relation_note: Differs in type from the catalog's existing statement (Wikipedia paraphrase of Heine 1976: stress system with 'primary' stress in any position and 'secondary' stress on the 2nd syllable in Nyang'i). Beer 2017, the only full description and the only primary source opened, finds no stress correlates independent of pitch, no lexical or grammatical pitch contrast, and analyses word prosody as lexically specified but non-contrastive H/L tone; he gives no stress position and no secondary stress. It agrees with the catalog only in that the word-level prominence pattern is lexical and unpredictable ('pitch features.. are unpredictable'), so a reader could file it as lexical (unpredictable) pitch ra…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated. Each root carries a lexically specified, unpredictable pitch melody built from two underlying tones (H, L; surface H, L and word-final falling = H+L on the last syllable), associated one-to-one left-to-right; pitch never creates a lexical contrast (no minimal pairs found), some plural suffixes impose replacive tone on the root. Beer finds no independent stress cues (duration, amplitude) beyond pitch and treats the system with tone formalism, leaving the stress-vs-tone label open ('not more meaningfully described as a stress system than as a tone system'). On p. 52: 'Nyang'i is the only language of the three [Ik, Soo, Nyang'i], then, that lacks contrastive pitch features.' On p. 4 he reports that Heine (1974/5)'s six pages of notes contain 'four phonetic pitches and notation for primary stress'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; no statement of primary or secondary stress position. The Wikipedia/Heine claim of secondary stress on the second syllable is neither confirmed nor mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Tendencies only: of 102 CV.CVC roots 59 take L.H, the rest L.L, H.F, H.H, H.L (p. 41-42); LH is the most frequent melody (54%) in the inherited-vocabulary sample (p. 61-62). Falling tone restricted to a closed final syllable. Replacive-tone plural suffixes (/-ík/, /-itín/ and six others) overlay L on the whole root.
new_statements.identity_note: Beer 2017 describes the contracted Nyang'i of a single remaining semi-speaker in Karamoja Region, Uganda (fieldwork 2012-13), and says explicitly that it is a description of a language in the final stage of death; Heine (1974/5, 1976) described the language from 1970s speakers. The ELAR deposit holds Weatherby's 1964-1972 Soo and Nyangi recordings/notes. Glottolog nyan1313 = Nyang'i [nyp], Kuliak; the Wikipedia statement names Nyang'i alongside Ik and Tepes (So/Soo).

readall_conflicts: One disagreement of type, not of placement. The catalog's existing statement (Wikipedia 'Kuliak languages', paraphrasing Heine 1976, no page) treats Nyang'i as a stress language: primary stress lexically placed in any position, secondary stress on the second syllable. Beer 2017 (§2.5, pp. 40-41; §2.1, p. 20; §2.6.3, p. 52), the only primary description opened, reports instead a lexically specified but non-contrastive two-tone (H/L) pitch system, finds that duration and amplitude do not pattern with pitch, states that the system 'is not more meaningfully described as a stress system than as a tone system', gives no stress position and no secondary stress, and says Nyang'i alone among Ik, Soo and Nyang'i lacks contrastive pitch. Beer himself notes (p. 4) that Heine (1974/5)'s notes used 'four phonetic pitches and notation for primary stress', so Heine did mark stress; the two sources agree that word-level prominence is lexical and unpredictable, and differ on whether it is stress or (non-contrastive) tone. Beer's data are from a single semi-speaker of the contracted 2012-13 variety, which may account for part of the gap. The ELAR deposit is silent.
